title: Laplace's Equation
body:
$$
\nabla^2 u = \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = 0
$$

Steady state. No time variable at all: this is what the [[Heat Equation]] becomes once $u_t = 0$,
so it describes the temperature distribution a system settles into, or an electrostatic potential
in a charge-free region, or the shape of a soap film on a wire loop.

Solutions are called **harmonic functions** and they have two properties worth carrying:

- **Mean value property**: the value at a point equals the average over any circle centred there.
  Nothing is hotter or colder than its surroundings on average, which is exactly what "settled" means
- **Maximum principle**: consequently, the maximum and minimum occur on the **boundary**, never in
  the interior. So the boundary conditions do not merely constrain the solution, they contain it

The operator $\nabla^2 = \nabla\cdot\nabla$ is the [[Divergence]] of the [[Gradient]], called the
Laplacian. With a nonzero right hand side, $\nabla^2u = f$, it is Poisson's equation.

The discrete version is a stencil: each grid point equals the average of its four neighbours. That
turns the PDE into a large sparse [[System of Linear Equations]], which is how it is actually
solved on a computer, and it is the same averaging step that image-processing blurs and mesh
smoothing use. See [[Image Processing]].
